list.listitem: Order emergent neuroimaging if the child has a focal deficit that does not resolve or if he or she does not return to baseline mental status. B
Consider neuroimaging if focal or prolonged seizure, baseline neurological deficits of unknown cause, abnormal EEG, or age less than 1 year. B
Order EEG for unprovoked seizures as an outpatient to help define prognosis and identify potential epileptic syndromes. C
Consider antiepileptic drug treatment after second seizure or after a first seizure if child has a syndrome or lesion that puts him or her at high risk for seizure recurrence. B
The family and child should follow seizure precautions for at least 6 to 12 months after the first seizure. C

background.definition: A seizure is a paroxysmal clinical event of the CNS, characterized by an abnormal electrical discharge and associated with a change in usual functioning. Epilepsy is defined as two or more unprovoked seizures in a child over 1 month of age.

list.listitem: 25,000 to 40,000 children experience their first unprovoked seizure each year in the United States, 89 to 134/100,000 person years.
Incidence is highest in children <1 year old (118/100,000), plateaus in childhood (46/100,000 age 1-10 years), and is lower in adolescents (21/100,000).
1% of children will have at least one afebrile seizure by age 14 years.
0.5% to 1.0% of children aged 1 to 16 years has epilepsy.
A systematic review concluded that the point prevalence is 5.2/1000 children age 0 to 9 years, and 8.9/1000 children age 10 to 19 years.

The differential diagnosis for new-onset seizure is broad and highly dependent on the clinical situation; 20% to 30% of first seizures are "provoked" by an acute brain insult or metabolic or toxic disturbance of brain function.
Acute symptomatic: causes include meningitis, encephalitis, trauma, intoxication, electrolyte disturbance, hypoglycemia, hemorrhage, tumor, acute ischemic stroke, syncope, and febrile seizure.

Remote symptomatic: causes include past brain injury, brain malformation, chronic metabolic/mitochondrial disorder, history of ischemic infarct, genetic syndrome (e.g., Retts, tuberous sclerosis, any chromosomal abnormality), and unknown disorders causing developmental delay/static encephalopathy or other neurologic symptoms.
Genetic: channelopathy, familial epilepsy syndrome (e.g., SCN1a mutation, GEFS+, childhood absence epilepsy).
Cryptogenic: cause unknown; no other neurological abnormalities.
Risk factors for seizure include cerebral palsy, mental retardation, and family history of epilepsy.
Seizures are caused by an imbalance of excitatory and inhibitory impulses in the brain, tipping the balance to abnormal excitatory stimulation.
Epileptic seizures result from specific abnormal patterns of excitability and synchrony among neurons in select brain areas, usually but not necessarily involving cortex.
Seizures can be caused by almost any acute or chronic cerebral insult.

Seizure prophylaxis is not routinely recommended after moderate to severe traumatic brain injury. If used, levetiracetam may be somewhat more effective than phenytoin for early onset seizures but with no impact on mortality.B
Important history includes whether this seizure was provoked, child's prior seizure history, and description of seizure (focal or generalized). C
Workup depends on clinical circumstances (). C
Order emergent neuroimaging for children with a focal deficit that does not resolve or prolonged altered mental status. B

Consider neuroimaging (preferably MRI) in patients with focal seizure, prolonged seizure, neurodevelopmental abnormalities, abnormality on neurological exam, or abnormal EEG that is not consistent with a known epilepsy syndrome, or in any patient under 1 year of age. B

Differential.Differential_Features: May be preceded by typical visual disturbance or feeling of lightheadedness
Event occurring in the setting of breath-holding or crying
May be difficult to differentiate from epileptic seizure; may be characterized by pelvic thrusting, random thrashing movements, tight eye closure during and after event
Vomiting, events occurring after or with feeds in infants
No alteration of consciousness; may be consciously suppressed; less common in sleep
May have stereotyped or self-gratification behavior; no loss of consciousness; often occur in a particular setting
Can be interrupted by stimulation; less likely to occur during active or enjoyable activities
Movements occur in early stages of sleep; not usually associated with neurological impairments

list.listitem: Over 95% of seizures are self-limited and last for less than 5 minutes. Up to one-third of children initially presumed to have had their first seizure had evidence of prior seizures on detailed history.

History: Obtain a description of the seizure: focal vs. generalized, preservation vs. loss of consciousness, length of event. Children with a focal seizure are at higher risk of having an abnormality on neuroimaging than children with a generalized seizure. Also carefully inquire about any history of prior seizures, either convulsive or nonconvulsive (i.e., absence). Typical presentation of seizure subtypes is shown in .

Associated symptoms: Was seizure provoked or unprovoked? Precipitating factors may include fever, infection, trauma, intoxication, metabolic disturbance. Any signs of gastroenteritis? Infectious gastroenteritis has been associated with seizure occurrence.

Other history: History of other neurological abnormalities, developmental delay or cerebral palsy? Children with other neurological or neurodevelopmental deficits are at a higher risk for seizures and seizure recurrence than typically developing children.
Family history of seizures or neurological disease? There are familial neurological syndromes that will increase the risk of seizure recurrence.
Physical examination: Look for signs of cause of seizure: fever, trauma, rash, nuchal rigidity, neurocutaneous stigmata, papilledema, retinal changes, syndromic features, hepatosplenomegaly.
Perform a thorough neurological exam, including mental status, and look for any localizing signs, including weakness, numbness, speech abnormalities, visual changes, reflex asymmetry, or ataxia.
In hospitalized children with head injury, the presence of seizures (LR+ 3.9) increases the likelihood that it is the result of physical abuse.
Laboratory studies should be ordered based on clinical circumstances including findings of illness, failure to return to baseline mental status, or young age (especially <1 year).
If patient is less than 1 year of age, order glucose, electrolytes, calcium, and magnesium (at a minimum) as soon as the child presents for evaluation.

If there is no return to baseline mental status, order glucose, electrolytes, calcium, magnesium, neuroimaging, and urine toxicology emergently. Consider lumbar puncture (LP) for bacterial or viral meningoencephalitis; consider other traumatic, metabolic, or toxic causes of altered mental status (liver failure, renal failure, toxic exposure, infection).
If there is any suspicion of possible drug exposure, order urine toxicology as soon as child presents for medical care. If there is any possibility of pregnancy, order beta-HCG.

If there is a suspicion of meningitis or encephalitis, or if the child is very young (<6 months), consider urgent LP for CSF bacterial culture and PCR for herpes simplex virus. CT should be obtained prior to LP if there is any suspicion for increased intracranial pressure. In most children >6 months with their first complex febrile seizure without signs/symptoms of meningitis, an LP will be negative (99%).

EEG is recommended in all children after the first unprovoked seizure to predict the risk of recurrence and to classify seizure type and epilepsy syndrome, but optimal timing of EEG remains unclear. EEG in the first 48 hours after a seizure may have transient abnormalities and must be interpreted with caution, but may be helpful if it is unclear whether event was truly an epileptic seizure. Authors of a Cochrane Review found no RCTs as evidence to support or refute the use of EEGs and its timing after complex febrile seizures among children.

Obtain neuroimaging if seizure was focal, if the child has ongoing neurological deficits, if the child does not return to baseline mental status in the hour after seizure, if there is a suspicion of significant head trauma or abnormal EEG, or if patient is <1 year old. MRI is the neuroimaging study of choice; CT is often used emergently. CT scan can detect hemorrhage, hydrocephalus, mass effect, significant cerebral edema, and calcifications, but can miss tumors and cerebral malformations. Always consider the risk of sedation if needed to obtain the study.
In the ICU, continuous EEG monitoring is more likely to detect seizures and is most commonly used post cardiac arrest, with CNS infection, or after status epilepticus.
Children taking anti-seizure medications commonly have mild leukopenia, but clinical impact is generally minimal.

A clinical prediction rule has been developed in a group of 451 children who were evaluated for a paroxysmal event and who had at least one year of follow-up. A model incorporating sex, age, a description of the event, the medical history, and the EEG was developed and has an AUC of 0.86 and positive and negative predictive values of 93% and 76% respectively. It was successfully validated in a prospective cohort of 186 patients and is available as an online calculator here.
See for a suggested approach to evaluation.
A clinical prediction rule has been developed in 451 children presenting with paroxysmal events and possible seizure and validated in a separate group of 187.
First unprovoked seizure does not necessarily require antiepileptic drug treatment. A
Consider antiepileptic drug treatment after a second seizure or after a first seizure if child has a syndrome or lesion that puts him or her at high risk for seizure recurrence. B
If the first seizure was prolonged, consider prescribing rectal diazepam for emergent future use to treat seizures lasting longer than 5 minutes. C
The family and child should follow seizure precautions for at least 6 to 12 months after a first seizure. C

AAN guidelines (reaffirmed in 2024) state that no chronic treatment is recommended in most cases if the event was truly the first seizure. Consider chronic treatment after one seizure if the patient is at very high risk for seizure recurrence and/or if a seizure recurrence could seriously jeopardize the child's health.
Consider a prescription for rectal lorazepam or diazepam and teaching on its use if the initial seizure was prolonged. There is some evidence that rectal lorazepam is more effective.
If the child has epilepsy (repeated unprovoked seizures), specific treatment depends on the epilepsy syndrome (see below).

2018 guidelines from AAN regarding new anti-epileptic drugs recommend that lamotrigine may be considered as a treatment for new onset seizure. Vigabatrin and pregabalin are not recommended as initial therapy. They describe the evidence as "lacking to support or refuse" use of newer third generation anti-epileptic drugs such as felbamate, clobazam, and vigabatrin.
AAN guidelines also recommend that for treatment resistant generalized tonic clonic seizures and treatment resistant myoclonic epilepsy, levetiracetam should be considered as add-on therapy.

Choice of medication will depend on clinical circumstances and discussion with child and parents about efficacy and side effects. Among less expensive treatment options, carbamazapine and phenytoin are generally preferred to phenobarbital, largely because of fewer adverse effects. Systematic reviews comparing phenytoin and carbamazepine, phenytoin and valproate, or carbamazepine and valproate as initial monotherapy for epilepsy found no notable differences in efficacy between the drugs.

Treatment options for specific epilepsy syndromes are described below. If the epilepsy syndrome is unknown, then provider should choose a medication that can treat either focal or generalized epilepsy (e.g., levetiracetam, lamotrigine, zonisamide, valproic acid, topiramate, or phenobarbital).

A systematic review of 15 studies (n=1533 children) assessing the efficacy of pharmacologic agents in treating epilepsy in children under 3 years of age found that levetiracetam appears to be more effective than valproate, phenobarbital, or no therapy in decreasing seizures or stopping them altogether. However, the authors were unable to draw conclusions regarding the efficacy of other agents (topiramate, lamotrigine, phenytoin, vigabatrin, rufinamide, or stiripentol).

Options include carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, levetiracetam, lamotrigine, valproic acid (higher risk of hepatotoxicity in children <2 years old), topiramate, zonisamide, phenobarbital, gabapentin, phenytoin, lacosamide, and tiagabine.
Options include ethosuxamide, levetiracetam, lamotrigine, zonisamide, valproic acid (higher risk of hepatotoxicity in children <2 years old), topiramate, or phenobarbital.

A systematic review of five studies of lamotrigine vs. carbamazepine for partial-onset or generalized tonic-clonic seizures found that, although lamotrigine was less likely to be withdrawn, carbamazepine may be more effective.
An individual patient meta-analysis found that phenytoin was more effective than phenobarbitone in children or adults with generalized seizures.
A second individual patient meta-analysis concluded that there was no clear difference in efficacy between phenytoin and carbamazepine.

Ethosuxamide, valproate, and lamotrigine are commonly used. A randomized trial of 453 children compared ethosuximide, lamotrigine and valproic acid. After 16 weeks, the "freedom from failure" rates were better for ethosuximide (53%) and valproic acid (58%) than for lamotrigine (29%). The same study found less "attentional dysfunction" with ethosuximide (33% vs. 49%, p = 0.03). Thus, ethosuximide would be a good first choice based on efficacy and adverse effects. A randomized trial of 382 children compared ethosuximide, lamotrigine, and valproic acid and found that pre-treatment behavioral problems were worsened in children taking valproic acid than ethosuximide, reinforcing ethosuximide as a preferred initial therapy.

A systematic review found that high-dose ACTH is most effective. Low-dose has similar efficacy to high-dose corticosteroids. Vigabatrin (Sabril) is another option, though there have been concerns about visual field losses associated with vigabatrin.

Authors of a Cochrane review found that the optimal treatment of infantile spasms is unclear, though hormonal treatment (ACTH or prednisolone) resolves spasms in more patients than vigabatrin and may improve long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes in children with no identifiable cause for their infantile spasm.

For seizures in neonates, there is only limited evidence for the effectiveness of phenobarbital and phenytoin. An RCT showed that phenobarbital was more effective than levetiracetam in keeping neonates seizure-free within the first 24 hours after initiation (80% with phenobarbital vs 28% with levetiracetam, p <0.001; NNT = 2), but was also associated with more adverse effects.

A study identified 275 patients age 2 to 55 years with Lennox-Gastaut syndrome with 2 or more seizures per week and randomized them to cannabidiol 20 mg, cannabidiol 10 mg, or placebo. The median percent reduction in seizures from baseline was 42% in the 20 mg dose group, 37% in the 10 mg group, and 17% in the placebo group. Adverse events such as somnolence, diarrhea, and decreased appetite were more common in the 20 mg dose group.
A cost-effectiveness study concluded that use of cannabidiol is cost-effective for Lennox-Gastaut syndrome.

Vigabatrin, tigabine, topiramate, pregabalin, and zonisamide as an add-on therapy can reduce seizure frequency by 50% in people with drug-resistant partial epilepsy (vigabatrin RR: 2.58; 95% CI: 1.87-3.57; tigabine RR: 3.16; 95% CI: 1.97-5.07; topiramate RR: 2.97; 95% CI: 2.38-3.72, pregabalin RR: 2.61; 95% CI: 1.70-4.01; zonisamide RR: 1.92; 95% CI: 1.52-2.42), but can also lead to side effects that lead to drug discontinuation (vigabatrin RR: 2.49; 95% CI: 1.05-5.88; tigabine RR: 1.81; 95% CI: 1.25-2.62; topiramate RR: 2.44; 95% CI: 1.64-3.62, pregabalin RR: 1.39; 95% CI: 1.13-1.72, zonisamide RR: 1.64; 95% CI: 1.20-2.25).

A Cochrane review concluded that for patients not well controlled with a single agent, add-on therapy using losigamone was more likely to result in a reduction in seizure frequency, but also with more treatment withdrawals. In patients with poorly controlled focal epilepsy, gabapentin is effective as add-on therapy.

One study found no evidence that routine antiepileptic drug serum monitoring in order to reach predefined target serum drug levels helped patients achieve better seizure control in patients on antiepileptic monotherapy.

A Cochrane review found that IV lorazepam is as efficacious as IV diazepam in the treatment of acute tonic clonic seizures in children (RR: 1.09; 95% CI: 0.77-1.54) and is associated with fewer side effects (RR: 3.17; 95% CI: 1.63-6.14). A RCT of 273 children with status epilepticus found equal efficacy of IV lorazepam and IV diazepam, but less sedation with IV lorazepam (67% vs. 50%; NNTH = 6). Where intravenous access is not available, one study found that buccal midazolam is more effective than rectal lorazepam (RR: 2.05; 95% CI: 1.45-2.91). A multicenter study in 33 emergency departments found that IM diazepam is more efficacious than IV lorazepam in the treatment of patients (>13 kg, mean age 43 years) with seizure >5 minutes (73% vs. 63%, p <0.05; NNT = 10).

An RCT recruited 385 patients with status epilepticus unresponsive to benzodiazepines and randomized them to valproate, fosphenytoin, or levetiracetam. All were effective in just under half of patients and had similar adverse effect profiles.

In children not responsive to first-line treatment of status epilepticus, a report of two randomized trials found that levetiracetam and phenytoin were similarly effective, but found more hypotension with phenytoin.

Epilepsy surgery may be an option for those with intractable partial epilepsy. A RCT with 80 adult patients with intractable temporal lobe epilepsy found that more patients in the surgical group had improved quality of life measurements at 6 and 12 months compared to those in the medical group (62% vs. 17%; p <0.001; NNT for meaningful improvement in QOL at 6 months ranged from 2.0 for QOLIE-31 to 13.8 for SF-36 PCS).

A meta-analysis of 258 studies addressing effectiveness of pediatric epilepsy surgery at 12-month follow-up showed that surgery achieved higher seizure freedom than medical therapy (OR: 6.5; 95% CI: 2.9-14.7), but efficacy declined with time following the surgery with 64.8% seizure-free at 1 year (95% CI: 51.2%-76.4%), 60.3% seizure-free at 5 years (95% CI: 52.9%-67.4%), and 39.7% seizure-free at 10 years (95% CI: 28.4%-52.2%).

Vagal nerve stimulator is another option to treat medically intractable seizures. A systematic review found the high-stimulation paradigm was more effective than low stimulation (OR: 1.93; 95% CI: 1.1-3.4). Adverse effects may include hoarseness, pain, paresthesias, cough, and dyspnea.
A systematic review of 12 studies concluded that resective surgery was more likely to be successful with a shorter duration of epilepsy prior to surgery. The certainty was classified as low.
Authors of a Cochrane Review of 2 low-quality studies with 50 patients found that yoga as an adjunct to antiepileptics may be beneficial in control of seizures.
Acupuncture is not effective, although the number and quality of studies are limited.
There is no evidence to support the effectiveness of vitamins for seizure disorders.
There is not enough evidence to support the effectiveness of IVIG for seizure disorders.
There is not enough evidence to support the effectiveness of traditional Chinese medicine, psychological therapy, or melatonin for seizure disorders.

A randomized study of 120 children with Dravet syndrome found that the addition of cannabidiol oral solution (20 mg/kg/d) as an adjunct therapy to antiepileptics decreased the frequency of total seizures (p = 0.03) compared to placebo, with more adverse events reported in the cannabidiol group.
A systematic review of six studies of cannabidiol vs placebo for epilepsy found that cannabidiol is effective in decreasing seizure frequency compared to placebo (p<0.00001).
Neuropsychological evaluation can be helpful to identify cognitive disturbances in children with epilepsy.
Although hypnosis and other behavioral therapies have been used for children with nonepileptic "seizures," evidence of their effectiveness is weak.
Behavioral interventions may be helpful for comorbid anxiety or depression but do not appear to reduce seizure frequency.

A systematic review included 7 studies evaluating self-management education programs for children with epilepsy and their families, finding highly variable results. While some programs appeared to reduce seizure frequency, others had no effect, and individual study methods were problematic.

Ketogenic diet or a modified Atkins diet are options for children under 3 years of age with epilepsy and for those with medically intractable epilepsy, although evidence comes from primarily observational studies of varying quality.

One study of 102 children with daily seizures despite at least 3 antiepileptic medications found a decrease in seizure frequency after 3 months of eating a modified Atkins diet (59% of baseline seizures [95% CI: 44%-75%] in diet group vs. 96% [95% CI: 82%-109%]).

Children with epilepsy should be treated with an antiepileptic medication until they are seizure free for at least 18 months, but decisions about treatment length should be based on individual clinical circumstances and shared decision making with the parents.
The American Academy of Neurology recommends against medication withdrawal in children with abnormal electroencephalograms.
For children who are seizure-free for at least 2 years, there is insufficient evidence to recommend slow versus rapid tapering of anti-epileptic medications.
Children with a first seizure should be hospitalized if seizures continue, if they do not return to baseline mental status, or if the cause of the seizure requires hospitalization.
Strongly consider referral to a pediatric neurologist if the EEG is abnormal, if patient has repeated seizures, or if patient has other neurological deficits.
For children with first cryptogenic seizure, recurrence risk is 30% at 2 years. If the seizure occurred while awake and EEG is normal, recurrence risk is 20%. B

Most recurrences occur in the first 6 months (53%); 88% occur in the first 2 years after the initial seizure. Patients >16 years old who were seizure free for >6 months after an initial seizure have a <20% chance of a subsequent seizure regardless of treatment or lack of treatment.B

Risk factors for recurrence include remote symptomatic etiology (OR: 2.2), abnormal EEG (OR: 2.3), prior febrile seizures in patients with remote symptomatic etiology (OR: 2.7), family history of seizure and abnormal EEG in cryptogenic seizure (OR: 3.5), age <3 years with remote symptomatic seizure (OR: 2.8), and cryptogenic seizure occurring in sleep (OR: 1.9). B

While routine monitoring of serum anti-epileptic levels is usually recommended, a single RCT with 180 patients found no difference after 12 months in seizure rates or adverse effects with or without monitoring. B

People with childhood epilepsy (particularly if epilepsy was secondary to serious neurologic insult) who do not go into remission are at an increased risk (6.9/1000 patient years) of sudden unexplained death and all-cause death, according to a cohort study who followed 245 children with epilepsy for up to 40 years. B

cell.label: Patient stable and no longer seizing
History consistent with acute symptomatic seizure?
Work up provoking factor as appropriate; may include glucose, brain CT/MRI, toxicology screen, electrolytes, LP, CBC, metabolic screening, infectious workup.
Is patient back to baseline mental status?
Other cause of altered mental status? Consider toxicology screen, metabolic labs, LP, neurology consult, EEG.
Brain MRI (If patient returns to baseline quickly, may be done as an outpatient).
Observe, outpatient workup as indicated: EEG, neurology outpatient visit.
Observe, outpatient workup as indicated: EEG, consider nonemergent MRI.
Stabilize patient (ABCs) and treat status epilepticus.

feature.caption: Common Seizures.
feature.feature_body:
Seizure Type Description Possible Syndrome
Generalized tonic clonic seizure Loss of consciousness; often rhythmic jerking of extremities; eyes usually open; may have grunting vocalizations, salivation Partial epilepsy (with secondary generalization), primary generalized, provoked seizure
Absence seizure Staring spells; eye blinking, behavioral arrest; usually last <20 seconds; occurs independent of patient's current activity Primary generalized or partial/focal seizure; usually patient has had past events by the time of presentation to medical care
Focal/partial seizure Transient abnormal function of area controlled by affected area of brain, including rhythmic jerking/twitching of body part, dysarthria, aphasia, behavior arrest, eye deviation, visual hallucinations, head turn, focal altered sensory function; may or may not lead to altered mental status Partial/focal epilepsy or provoked seizure; may progress to a generalized seizure
Myoclonic seizure Brief jerk of one or more extremities; consciousness often preserved; drop attacks may also be negative myoclonus Primary generalized epilepsy; unlikely to be a single event at the time of presentation to medical care
Nonepileptic event May be characterized by tight eye closure, pelvic thrusting, preserved consciousness, with prolonged involvement of right and left body parts Consider psychosocial stressors and conversion disorder, although patients with nonepileptic seizures may also have true epileptic seizures as well
Data from Engel J, Jr. Report of the ILAE classification core group. Epilepsia 2006;47:1558–1568.
